title: Introduction to philosophy
audience: a high-school student (grades 9–12) or an adult reviewing high-school work
purpose: Study the main areas of philosophy at a first-year college level: logic and argument, the beginnings of philosophy in Greece and around the world, epistemology, metaphysics, philosophy of mind, free will, philosophy of religion, value theory, ethics and political philosophy, reading primary texts closely and writing argumentative essays.

weeks.1: What philosophy is and how it works
weeks.2: Logic and argument: validity, soundness and strength
weeks.3: Socrates, Plato and Aristotle: how philosophy began in Greece
weeks.4: Philosophy around the world: India, China, Africa and the Islamic world
weeks.6: Metaphysics: substance, universals and the nature of reality
weeks.7: Philosophy of mind: dualism, physicalism and consciousness
weeks.9: Philosophy of religion: arguments about God and the problem of evil
weeks.11: Normative ethics: consequences, duties and virtues
weeks.12: Political philosophy: justice, rights and the state

blocks.deliverable: Reconstruct three arguments in standard form.
Compare two traditions' answers to one question.
Explain a skeptical argument and evaluate one reply.
Week 7 midterm; write a short essay on the mind-body problem.
Reconstruct an argument for God's existence and an objection.
Submit the project; take an unseen 60 minute final in week 14.

project: Argumentative essay: choose one question from the course, read two short primary texts (public-domain or free online) that answer it differently, reconstruct each argument in standard form, and write a 1,500-word essay that defends an answer and replies to the strongest objection.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.
